The power consumption of a frequency comb is directly related to the (small) pulse energy required to detect the carrier-envelope offset frequency (fCEO) of the pulsed source. Typically, fCEO detection requires sufficient pulse energy to generate an octaves panning spectrum and second harmonic generation (SHG) of the red end of the spectrum. This drives the optical power requirement, and hence power consumption, on the optical source (oscillator and often optical amplifier). Current technology involves a highly nonlinear optical fiber (HNLF) to broaden the spectrum and a nonlinear bulk crystal for frequency doubling. New technologies based on a Photonic Integrated Circuit (PIC) offers the prospect to substantially reduce this pulse energy (by factor of ten). Demonstration of a packaged, Carrier Envelope Offset frequency (fCEO) detection demonstrator unit with fiber in-coupling and fCEO electrical signalout which shall also take full advantage of any recent development enhancements in the capabilities of integrated photonics. Particular emphasis is taken to reduce the coupling losses into the optical waveguide to enhance the overall frequency conversion efficiency.The following tasks are foreseen in this activity: Development of a fCEO based on the new Lithium Niobate on Insulator (LNoI) or Lithium Niobate on Silicon Nitride (LNoSN) or any other competitive platforms. Provide a few possible design options to explore. Trade off the various designs to meet the primary goal of enhance efficiency and system simplification. Manufacture the final design for assembly and verification test at system level. Provide verification of the (10x) enhanced performance using bulk and waveguide technologies as demonstrators. Develop preliminary device packaging options, without sacrificing performance.
